turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, I'm the nurse. I'll just do your observations before the doctor comes in. Pop your arm out for me, thanks.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning. Yes, of course. I hope I have not kept you waiting.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Not at all. Blood pressure is 132 over 84, pulse 76, temperature 36.7, sats 98 percent on room air, and you're breathing at 16. All very respectable.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): That is reassuring, thank you. I have been rather anxious about this rash.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): The doctor won't be long. Your sister is still sorting the parking. She asked me to pass something on, but I'll wait and say it once the doctor's in the room.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): My sister does fuss. She means well, though she is not always accurate.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Shah. Come through. I can see you're uncomfortable. What's brought you in today?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, Doctor. I have developed a rather itchy rash, and I am uncertain whether it followed something I ate, a new cream, or the antibiotic.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, an itchy rash with three possible culprits. We'll unpack those one at a time. When did you first notice the rash?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, we had prawns at my sister's place on Saturday evening, and I had begun a new cream the evening before. The dentist started me on an antibiotic on Wednesday.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Those details matter, and we'll come back to each of them. The rash itself, though, which day did you actually first see it on your skin?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I beg your pardon, I did not answer you directly. It was Sunday morning, as I was dressing. I am confident of that.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sunday morning, so we're looking at several days, not hours. Where is the rash sitting?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Across my trunk, and it has spread onto both upper arms. It is red, and the itch is really quite insistent, particularly in the evening.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Insistent in the evening, heat of the bed often does that. Any swelling of the face or the lips, or any trouble getting your breath?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have had neither swelling nor any difficulty with my breathing.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. And have you felt feverish, or had any joint pains with it?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever, Doctor, and my joints have been quite comfortable.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): What about the mouth, ulcers, or a sore throat?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): My throat has been perfectly fine. The dental issue is the lower molar, not the throat.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tell me about that dental issue, since the antibiotic hangs off it.

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): The dentist diagnosed a dental abscess on Wednesday and prescribed amoxicillin. I have been taking it by mouth, I believe five hundred milligrams three times a day, though the bottle is at home and I may have the strength slightly wrong.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): So possibly 500 mg three times daily, not confirmed. Have you taken every dose?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): I am afraid not. I missed one dose on Friday, and I am not certain about Saturday morning. Otherwise I have been regular, including a dose this morning.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): All right, adherence a bit patchy, still on it as of this morning. Now the cream, what is it called?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I cannot recall the name, I am sorry. Um, it is a white cream in a tube from the chemist, with oatmeal in it, for dry skin. I have been putting it on my shins since Friday evening.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Oatmeal cream, name unknown, shins only. And the rash you describe is on the trunk and arms, not the shins?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): That is correct. The shins themselves are not involved, which I found puzzling. I stopped using the cream yesterday morning.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sensible to stop it. And the prawns, just the one meal?

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, a modest serving on Saturday evening. I have eaten prawns many times before without illness. My sister takes biotin tablets for her hair; she offered me one, but I declined. That is her medicine, not mine.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Noted, biotin is hers. I'm not going to put that on your list. Any other regular medicines of your own?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I take rosuvastatin, ten milligrams, at night, for my cholesterol. I have done so for some years. Nothing else.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Cholesterol, rosuvastatin 10 mg at night. Any allergies to medicines or anything else?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): None that I am aware of. I have taken penicillin on previous occasions without any reaction.

[SEG0035] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry to butt in, Doctor. His sister caught me in the corridor. She was quite firm that he came out in a rash with penicillin as a child, and the family have avoided it since. She wanted that written down.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I must respectfully disagree. I have no memory of any such episode, and I do not accept that account. My sister confuses me with our cousin at times.

[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): So we have a disagreement on the table. You deny a childhood penicillin reaction; your sister, via the nurse, reports a rash and subsequent avoidance. I can't resolve that from here, and I won't record it as a confirmed allergy.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. I would not wish an incorrect allergy to follow me about.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fair. Has anyone in the family got eczema or asthma, properly speaking, as their own condition?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): My sister has mild eczema. Our parents did not, to my knowledge. I myself have never had eczema.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sister with eczema, you without. I'm going to have a look now. Trunk and arms, you said.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, please. It is rather unsightly, I apologise.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): No need. There's a red, blotchy, maculopapular rash over the chest, abdomen and both upper arms, with a few scratch marks. The shins are clear, as you said.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): It does look angry in this light.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): Lips are not swollen. Mouth and throat look normal. I'm just listening to the chest.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Of course.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest is clear, no wheeze. While I'm looking at your face, the eyelids do look a little puffy to me. Had you noticed that?

[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): I should correct what I said earlier. I denied any swelling, but that was not accurate. My eyelids were puffy yesterday and they are still mildly swollen this morning. My lips have remained normal, and my breathing has been fine throughout.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thank you for correcting that. Mild eyelid swelling, lips spared, breathing spared. That nudges me a little, but it still isn't a classic immediate allergic picture.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): I felt I ought to be precise, even at the cost of contradicting myself.

[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): Precision helps. Let me think out loud. Three candidates. The amoxicillin started Wednesday, rash Sunday, so day four or so, which is a very typical window for a delayed drug eruption.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): I see. So the timing fits the antibiotic.

[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): It fits, it doesn't prove it. The cream started Friday, but you've put it only on the shins and the shins are clear, so a straightforward contact dermatitis is less likely, though I wouldn't completely throw it out if a bit got on your hands and then the trunk.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): I did wash my hands, though perhaps not immediately.

[SEG0055] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the prawns were Saturday night, rash noticed Sunday morning, which is a bit quick for some reactions and a bit slow for others. You've tolerated prawns before. So food is possible, not my favourite.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): I had wondered if it was the prawns, given how suddenly the itch declared itself.

[SEG0057] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to make a firm diagnosis today. My working impression is uncommitted: a delayed amoxicillin eruption sits at the top, a contact reaction from the unnamed cream is still possible, and I can't fully exclude the prawns.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. What would you advise I do?

[SEG0059] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'd like you to stop the amoxicillin from now. Don't take tonight's dose. Ring the dentist this afternoon and tell them you've developed a rash and I've asked you to hold it. We may need a different antibiotic if the tooth is still angry, but that's their call.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): I will telephone the dentist. The tooth is quieter than it was, thankfully.

[SEG0061] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. Leave the oatmeal cream off as well, which you've already done. For the itch I'll prescribe cetirizine, ten milligrams, one tablet by mouth once a day, for the next week or so.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): Will that make me drowsy? I have a board paper to finish.

[SEG0063] person_3 (DOCTOR): Cetirizine is one of the less sedating ones, though a few people still feel a bit foggy. If it bothers you, take it in the evening. I'm not starting a steroid cream today; I want to see the pattern without adding another topical.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): That seems prudent. And the penicillin question?

[SEG0065] person_3 (DOCTOR): I won't label you penicillin-allergic on your sister's say-so alone, especially as you've taken amoxicillin this week without an immediate collapse or lip swelling. But I also won't ignore her. If this rash is the drug, we'll revisit labelling once the dust settles.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): I am content with that approach.
[SEG0067] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the rash is still there in a fortnight, we might arrange patch testing for the cream, or a formal drug-allergy review. I'm not booking that today.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight seems a reasonable interval.

[SEG0069] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you back here in one week regardless, so I can look at the skin again. Sooner if your lips swell, if you become short of breath, or if the rash blisters or you feel very unwell.
[SEG0070] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall come back in one week, and I will not wait if those things occur.
[SEG0071] person_1 (NURSE): I can book that one-week review at the desk on your way out, if that suits.
[SEG0072] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, please, that would be helpful.
[SEG0073] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thanks. Also, skip prawns and any new creams or soaps until we've reviewed. Keep the rosuvastatin going, that isn't part of this.
[SEG0074] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall continue the rosuvastatin and avoid prawns and new products.

[SEG0075] person_3 (DOCTOR): Cool showers are fine for the itch, loose cotton, try not to scratch even though I know that's a tall order. If you need something for the tooth pain, paracetamol is all right, as directed on the packet. You haven't been taking any, have you?
[SEG0076] person_2 (PATIENT): I took two paracetamol tablets yesterday afternoon for the tooth, and none since. I am happy to use it again if required.
[SEG0077] person_3 (DOCTOR): One-off yesterday, not a regular medicine then. I won't add it to your usual list. Any questions?
[SEG0078] person_2 (PATIENT): Only whether I should bring the cream tube next time, so you can see the name.
[SEG0079] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, please bring the tube, and the amoxicillin bottle so we can confirm the strength. That would clear up both loose ends.
[SEG0080] person_2 (PATIENT): I will bring both. Thank you for your thoroughness, Doctor.
[SEG0081] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're welcome. Nurse will sort the script and the appointment. We'll see how much of this has faded in a week.

features: patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
